title: On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring in AI Governance
summary: Investigates how trusted execution environments (TEEs) could enable verification and monitoring in AI governance while preserving privacy, e.g. verifying compliance with AI agreements without fully exposing model/data internals.
key_result: TEEs are a plausible technical building block for privacy-preserving verification in international AI governance, enabling monitoring without full disclosure.
open_threads: Hardware/supply-chain trust assumptions, side-channel vulnerabilities, practical deployment at data-center scale.

title: Catching Illicit Distributed Training Operations During an AI Pause
summary: Explores whether covert distributed training of frontier models could undermine an internationally agreed AI development pause, and how such activity might be detected; assesses feasibility of clandestine distributed training and monitoring/verification options.
key_result: Covert distributed training is a credible evasion route around compute-restriction agreements, but leaves detectable signatures verification regimes could in principle catch.
open_threads: Detection robustness against obfuscated/dispersed training; false-positive rates; governance/enforcement mechanisms.

title: Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried
authors: Daniel Tan, J Bostock, David Africa et al. (Arcadia Alignment)
summary: Argues that deliberately induced pathologies in AI 'model organisms' often degrade the models in unrelated ways, making them unrealistic proxies for deployment; existing organisms lose preference coherence and instruction-following despite holding up on standard benchmarks.
key_result: Most model organisms dramatically lose preference coherence relative to base (large drops in a 'mu-decisiveness' metric), alongside broken reasoning traces and unprompted training-data leakage.
open_threads: Limited knowledge of real training pipelines; whether fixes preserve coherence; mu-decisiveness metric may be gameable; add coherence checks to evals.

title: Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence
authors: Vansh Gupta, Andreas Krause, Florian Tramer, Lukas Fluri, Anna Hedstrom et al.
summary: A position paper arguing much Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research (AMR) lacks the evidentiary rigor needed to inform high-stakes decisions; dissects failure modes across deception, emergent misalignment, and sycophancy, showing how conceptual ambiguity, non-robust datasets, weak experimental design, and insufficient causal interventions lead researchers to overinterpret model behaviors.
key_result: Claims about anthropomorphic AI risks frequently rest on weak evidence; the field needs shared, graduated evidentiary standards before such claims justify deployment or regulatory decisions.
open_threads: Adopt a framework of graduated 'evidence levels' and a diagnostic checklist; operationalize constructs like deception/sycophancy; build robust well-controlled datasets; use causal interventions (not just correlational probes); re-evaluate existing high-profile misalignment results against the checklist.
